title: New SECURE 2.0 rules will automatically enroll eligible workers in 401(k) and 403(b) plans unless they opt out

 Your Employer May Start Saving for Your Retirement Without Being Asked — Here's the Federal Rule Behind It
 Covered employers must default newly eligible employees into workplace retirement plans at a contribution rate of at least 3%, with several exemptions.
 Rebecca Montecinos 
/
 Published Nov 17 2026, 5:21 PM EST Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 A man walks past the US Treasury in Washington, DC, on February 6, 2025. Opponents to US President Donald Trump say he allowed Elon Musk -- the world's richest man and a major government contractor -- to break the law by accessing US Treasury payment systems that send out trillions of dollars and hold a welter of sensitive personal data. 
 Photo by Mandel NGAN / AFP) (Photo by MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images 
 The Briefing: 
 The Treasury Department and IRS have finalized regulations implementing SECURE 2.0's auto-enrollment mandate, requiring qualifying employers to default new eligible workers into 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans at a minimum 3% contribution rate. 
 Employees retain complete control — they can adjust their contribution percentage or opt out entirely at any time, with no penalty. 
 Treasury projects the mandate will add an average of $4.2 billion in additional annual retirement savings nationwide through 2032, targeting a coverage gap that affects roughly half of all private-sector workers. 
 The Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service issued final regulations Tuesday putting into binding effect a central retirement-savings provision of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 — one that requires qualifying employers to automatically sign newly eligible workers into workplace retirement plans rather than leaving enrollment as a step employees must take on their own. 
 The move is projected to generate an average of $4.2 billion in additional retirement contributions each year over the 2023–2032 period, according to Treasury's estimates — a figure that reflects just how many eligible workers have historically never gotten around to enrolling. 
 Four Years from Law to Regulation 
 When Congress passed the SECURE 2.0 Act in December 2022, it included a mandate — codified under Internal Revenue Code Section 414A — requiring newly established 401(k) and 403(b) plans to build automatic enrollment into their framework from the outset. The provision was set to take effect for plan years beginning after December 31, 2024, but employers have spent two years without clear implementing rules, operating on interim guidance and good-faith interpretations of the statute. 
 Tuesday's finalization, formally published as Treasury Decision 10061, ends that period of regulatory ambiguity. The final rules deliver the operational specificity that HR departments, retirement plan administrators, and employment attorneys have been waiting for — covering default rates, notice requirements, permissible withdrawals, and the precise scope of statutory exceptions. 
 How the Default Enrollment Mechanism Works 
 Under the new framework, covered employers must set an initial default contribution rate of at least 3% of compensation for all newly eligible employees. Workers who do nothing are enrolled automatically at that rate, with their contributions directed into a qualified default investment alternative. 
 The design is intentional and evidence-based. Research in behavioral economics has consistently shown that when retirement plan participation is the default rather than the goal, enrollment rates climb significantly — even in systems where opting out is straightforward. Workers who prefer a different contribution rate, want to redirect their savings to specific investment options, or would rather not participate at all may change or cancel their elections at any point. 
 Who Is Covered — and the Important Exceptions 
 The mandate applies to businesses, educational institutions, and nonprofit organizations whose retirement plans were established after December 29, 2022 — the date the SECURE 2.0 Act became law. Plans that were already in existence before that date are generally grandfathered and not subject to the new requirement. 
 The final regulations also define the statutory carve-outs with greater clarity than the law alone provided. Exempt from the mandate are plans sponsored by employers with 10 or fewer employees, plans in existence for less than three years, church plans, governmental plans, and SIMPLE 401(k) arrangements. For employers that do fall within the mandate's scope, the rules now offer a cleaner compliance roadmap than any prior guidance had delivered. 
 The Retirement Coverage Gap This Policy Targets 
 "A financially secure retirement is a cornerstone of the American Dream, and every worker deserves the opportunity to achieve it," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the announcement. 
 The statement frames the central problem the regulation is designed to address. Despite decades of employer-sponsored retirement plans being available across the economy, roughly half of private-sector workers in America have no such plan at all. Among those who do have access, many never complete enrollment — not because they object to saving, but because the step of signing up goes undone. Auto-enrollment removes that friction entirely for newly eligible employees at covered employers. 
 The Broader SECURE 2.0 Restructuring 
 Tuesday's announcement is one of two major SECURE 2.0 regulatory milestones now in force simultaneously. The mandatory Roth catch-up contribution rules that took effect January 1, 2026 require workers aged 50 and older who earned more than $145,000 in the prior year to route their catch-up contributions into after-tax Roth accounts, rather than reducing their current taxable income through traditional pre-tax contributions. Those regulations, finalized by the IRS in September 2025, apply to 401(k), 403(b), and 457(b) plans and reshape retirement planning strategy for higher-income earners. 
 The two regulatory waves address opposite ends of the savings spectrum. Auto-enrollment targets the coverage gap — bringing workers into retirement plans who might otherwise never open one. The Roth catch-up mandate targets high earners already saving aggressively, redirecting a portion of their contributions toward after-tax treatment. Together, they represent the most consequential restructuring of workplace retirement rules since the original SECURE Act of 2019. 
 The Compliance Window Employers Face Now 
 For plan administrators and HR departments, the finalization of these rules opens an immediate action window. Existing plan documents for covered plans may require amendment, default contribution rates and investment elections need to be validated against the new minimums, and participant notice procedures have been revised under the final rules. Industry guidance from ADP and other retirement plan service providers recommends engaging plan custodians and legal counsel promptly, as the broader SECURE 2.0 plan amendment deadline falls on December 31, 2026. 
 For workers, the action item is simpler: reviewing current retirement account elections now — before automatic changes take effect — is worth a few minutes of attention. For employees at covered employers who have never enrolled, that review may reveal a contribution has already begun on their behalf.
